passages.t: A word for Baruch: do not seek great things
passages.happening:
This is the word Jeremiah spoke to Baruch son of Neriah when Baruch wrote these words on a scroll at Jeremiah's dictation, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (verse 1). The LORD speaks to Baruch himself (verse 2).

Baruch had said that the LORD had added sorrow to his pain, that he was worn out with groaning and found no rest (verse 3).

God's answer: ‘Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted’ (verse 4). “But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking!” (verse 5). God will bring disaster on all flesh, ‘but wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Baruch was a scribe, a trained professional who could read and write in a world where many could not. He was Jeremiah's secretary, his legal witness and his public reader, and he was accused of influencing the prophet. His brother Seraiah was a high official who went to Babylon with King Zedekiah, so Baruch probably came from a family that could hope for advancement.

The date takes the reader back to 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish. For a young scribe, the future may have looked full of promise. Instead Baruch spent his life writing down a message of destruction and hiding from the king.

This short chapter is set after the story of the flight to Egypt, at the end of Jeremiah's own story. The last personal word in the account belongs to his faithful scribe.

God's words about demolishing what he built and uprooting what he planted use the verbs of Jeremiah's call. God himself is tearing down what he built. It is no time for Baruch to build his own name.
passages.later: A psalm prays, ‘I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me’ (Psalm 131:1). Ebed-melech was given the same promise, that he would ‘escape with your life like a spoil of war’ (Jeremiah 39:18).
passages.hard:
Is it wrong to want great things? Why does God tell Baruch to stop seeking them?

The text does not say exactly what the great things were. Some interpreters think Baruch hoped for a high position at court, like his brother; others think he hoped for relief, for the prophecies to be reversed, or for a reward for his faithfulness. The warning is set against national judgment: when God is tearing down the whole land, it makes no sense to build a personal empire. Read this way, the chapter is not a blanket condemnation of ambition but a word about timing and priorities. Others read it more widely, as a warning against seeking oneself in God's service at any time.

Both readings agree that God's answer to Baruch is not only a rebuke. It is a promise: his life will be kept wherever he goes.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Baruch was worn out and wanted more than God was giving. Ask what great things you are seeking for yourself right now. And ask whether you can receive your life itself, kept by God, as enough.
